Empirical Research Plan: “Why Has CEO Pay Risen So Much?”  

======================================================================
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables (IV) panel estimation.

Rationale  
• The core parameter of interest is the causal elasticity of CEO pay (log Compensation) with respect to firm size (log Market Capitalization).  
• Firm size is endogenous: talented CEOs may both raise firm value and be paid more; governance failures can simultaneously depress value and inflate pay, etc.  
• We can construct plausibly exogenous shocks to firm value that are outside the control of the CEO or the board—e.g., industry-level stock-market movements, global commodity-price shocks, and Bartik (shift–share) demand shocks.  
• These shocks satisfy the exclusion restriction if they affect CEO pay only through their impact on firm size; they provide continuous, heterogeneous treatment intensity well suited for IV.  

Formally, for firm i in year t:  

1st stage logSize_it = π Z_it  +  X_it β  +  μ_i  +  λ_t  +  ε_it  
2nd stage logPay_it = α ĥlogSize_it + X_it γ + μ_i + λ_t + u_it  

where Z_it is the instrument set, μ_i are firm fixed effects, and λ_t are year fixed effects.  

======================================================================
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
• Treatment variable (endogenous regressor):  
 T_it ≡ log(Market Cap_it)  (or log(Sales) in robustness tests).  

• Instrument(s) Z_it (constructed annually for every firm):  
  a. Industry-Shock Instrument:  
     Z1_it = Σ_j s_ij,1980 × Δlog(Global Industry Market Cap)_jt  
     where s_ij,1980 is firm i’s 1980 sales share in 4-digit SIC industry j.  
  b. Commodity-Price Instrument (for resource industries):  
     Z2_it = (% of Sales in commodity k)_i,1980 × Δlog(Commodity Price)_kt  
  c. Leave-one-out Industry Return:  
     Z3_it = Δlog(Industry Return)_−i,t (industry return excluding firm i).  

• Control group / counterfactual:  
  Firms whose predicted size changes little when the common shocks hit.  
  Because identification comes from differential exposure to the same shocks, no separate “treated” vs. “untreated” groups are required; the remaining firms act as the counterfactual through the first-stage variation.  

• Timing: annual panel 1978–2004 (longer for time-series extensions).  

======================================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
A1 Relevance: The instruments are strongly correlated with log Market Cap.  
 Plausibility: Large global industry or commodity shocks mechanically move firm values; first-stage F-stats above 10 are expected.  

A2 Exclusion: Instruments affect CEO pay only via firm size, not through other direct channels.  
 Plausibility:  
 • Industry-wide valuation shocks are unlikely to alter governance quality or contract form contemporaneously.  
 • CEO bonus formulas may contain performance metrics, but that channel operates through the firm’s market cap or profits—the very pathway we wish to capture.  

A3 Independence (instrument exogenous to CEO-specific unobservables):  
 With firm FE we purge time-invariant talent; year FE absorb macro trends that hit all firms; remaining variation should be orthogonal to shocks in managerial quality.  

A4 Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers):  
 Because U.S. CEOs rarely switch firms within a year and compensation committees focus on own-firm metrics, one firm’s shock should not directly alter another’s CEO pay.  

A5 Linear separability / constant elasticity within the relevant range:  
 We assume a log-linear relationship; will check for non-linearities.  

======================================================================
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
T1 Performance-pay channel violates exclusion (industry shocks raise option values even without changing size).  
 Fix: Re-estimate using (i) salary + bonus only, (ii) equity grants valued at grant-date expected value rather than Black–Scholes, (iii) exclude option-heavy years (late-1990s).  

T2 Governance co-moves with industries (e.g., tech boom coincides with different boards).  
 Fix: Control flexibly for the GIM governance index, interact governance with year dummies, and add firm-specific linear time trends.  

T3 Anticipatory effects (boards foresee shocks and pre-set pay).  
 Fix: Use truly unexpected shocks—e.g., ex-post return surprises relative to analyst forecasts; instrument with t−1 to t innovations; show no pre-trend in placebo leads.  

======================================================================
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Load packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast FE & IV
library(lmtest)      # coeftest, waldtest
library(sandwich)    # vcovHC

#--------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data loading
#--------------------------------------------------
execu  <- fread("execucomp_1992_2004.csv")   # CEO pay
comp   <- fread("compustat_1978_2004.csv")   # firm financials
gov    <- fread("gim_index.csv")             # governance data
indret <- fread("global_industry_returns.csv")  # industry shocks
comm   <- fread("commodity_price_shocks.csv")   # commodity shocks

# Merge and keep needed vars
setkey(execu, gvkey, fyear)
setkey(comp,  gvkey, fyear)
df <- merge(execu, comp, by = c("gvkey","fyear"))
df <- merge(df, gov,  by = c("gvkey","fyear"), all.x = TRUE)
df <- merge(df, indret, by = c("sic4","fyear"), all.x = TRUE)
df <- merge(df, comm,  by = c("gvkey","fyear"), all.x = TRUE)

#--------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
#--------------------------------------------------
df[, `:=`(
  logPay   = log(TDC1 / gdp_deflator),               # real compensation
  logSize  = log((mkt_cap) / gdp_deflator),          # real firm size
  Z1       = sales_share80 * dlog_global_indval,     # Bartik instrument
  Z2       = commodity_share80 * dlog_comm_price,
  Z3       = leave_out_indret
)]
# Drop missing
df <- df[!is.na(logPay) & !is.na(logSize) & !is.na(Z1)]

#--------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main IV specification
#--------------------------------------------------
iv_eq <- feols(logPay ~ 1 | logSize ~ Z1 + Z2 + Z3,
               data = df,
               fixef = c("gvkey","fyear"),
               cluster = "gvkey")

summary(iv_eq)

#--------------------------------------------------
# 4. First-stage F-test
#--------------------------------------------------
wald(iv_eq, c('fit_Z1=0','fit_Z2=0','fit_Z3=0'))     # weak IV test

#--------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: compensation excluding options
#--------------------------------------------------
df[, logPay_noopt := log((salary + bonus + rstr_stock) / gdp_deflator)]

iv_rob <- feols(logPay_noopt ~ 1 | logSize ~ Z1 + Z2 + Z3,
                data = df, fixef = c("gvkey","fyear"),
                cluster = "gvkey")
summary(iv_rob)
```

======================================================================
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory of competitive assignment (Gabaix, 2014) predicts an elasticity ≈ 1: a 1 % increase in firm size raises the reservation wage of the marginal CEO by ~1 %. Prior empirical work finds OLS elasticities around 0.3–0.5; IV should be larger if OLS is attenuated by measurement error and reverse causality.  
My prior: α ≈ 0.8–1.0. Thus the sixfold (≈ log 6 ≈ 1.8) increase in average firm size from 1980–2003 can explain most of the sixfold increase in CEO pay.  

======================================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV)  
----------------------------------------------------------------------
C1 Instrument relevance:                   1  
C2 Exclusion restriction credible:        0.5  
C3 Independence from unobservables:       0.5  
C4 No weak-instrument problem (F>10):     1  
C5 Correct functional form / no effect heterogeneity biasing LATE: 0.5  

Total (out of 5): 3.5  

======================================================================
This plan would allow us to quantify how much of the level and growth of U.S. CEO compensation is mechanically accounted for by changes in firm scale versus alternative explanations rooted in governance or rent extraction.
